content.heading: 5.5 Complex Eigenvalues
content.paragraph: Since the characteristic equation of an $n \times n$ matrix involves a polynomial of degree $n$, the equation always has exactly $n$ roots, counting multiplicities, provided that possibly complex roots are included. This section shows that if the characteristic equation of a real matrix $A$ has some complex roots, then these roots provide critical information about $A$. The key is to let $A$ act on the space $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ of $n\text{-tuples}$ of complex numbers.1

Our interest in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ does not arise from a desire to “generalize” the results of the earlier chapters, although that would in fact open up significant new applications of linear algebra.2 Rather, this study of complex eigenvalues is essential in order to uncover “hidden” information about certain matrices with real entries that arise in a variety of real-life problems. Such problems include many real dynamical systems that involve periodic motion, vibration, or some type of rotation in space.

The matrix eigenvalue–eigenvector theory already developed for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ applies equally well to $\text{ℂ}^{n}$. So a complex scalar $\text{λ}$ satisfies $\text{det}(A - \text{λ}I) = 0$ if and only if there is a nonzero vector $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ such that $A\textbf{x} = \text{λ}\textbf{x}$. We call $\text{λ}$ a (complex) eigenvalue and $\textbf{x}$ a (complex) eigenvector corresponding to $\text{λ}$.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 0 & {- 1} \\ 1 & 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$, then the linear transformation $\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$ on $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ rotates the plane counterclockwise through a quarter-turn. The action of $A$ is periodic, since after four quarter-turns, a vector is back where it started. content.heading: Real and Imaginary Parts of Vectors
content.paragraph: The complex conjugate of a complex vector $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ is the vector $\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$ in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ whose entries are the complex conjugates of the entries in $\textbf{x}$. content.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix whose entries are real. Then $\overset{‾}{A\textbf{x}} = \overset{‾}{A}\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}} = A\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$. If $\text{λ}$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ and $\textbf{x}$ is a corresponding eigenvector in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$, then

Hence $\overset{‾}{\text{λ}}$ is also an eigenvalue of $A$, with $\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$ a corresponding eigenvector. This shows that when$A$is real, its complex eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. (Here and elsewhere, we use the term complex eigenvalue to refer to an eigenvalue $\text{λ} = a + bi$, with $b \neq 0$.)

Here is the rotation “inside” $A$! The matrix $P$ provides a change of variable, say, $\textbf{x} = P\textbf{u}$. The action of $A$ amounts to a change of variable from $\textbf{x}$ to $\textbf{u}$, followed by a rotation, and then a return to the original variable. See Figure 4. The rotation produces an ellipse, as in Figure 1, instead of a circle, because the coordinate system determined by the columns of $P$ is not rectangular and does not have equal unit lengths on the two axes.

content.paragraph: The next theorem shows that the calculations in Example 7 can be carried out for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ having a complex eigenvalue $\text{λ}$. The proof uses the fact that if the entries in $A$ are real, then $A\left( \text{Re~}\textbf{x} \right) = \text{Re}\left( A\textbf{x} \right)$ and $A\left( \text{Im~}\textbf{x} \right) = \text{Im}\left( A\textbf{x} \right)$, and if $\textbf{x}$ is an eigenvector for a complex eigenvalue, then $\text{Re~}\textbf{x}$ and $\text{Im~}\textbf{x}$ are linearly independent in $\textbf{R}^{2}$. (See Exercises 29 and 30.) The details are omitted.

content.paragraph: The phenomenon displayed in Example 7 persists in higher dimensions. For instance, if $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue, then there is a plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ on which $A$ acts as a rotation (possibly combined with scaling). Every vector in that plane is rotated into another point on the same plane. We say that the plane is invariant under $A$.

statement.paragraph: Let $A$ be a complex (or real) $n \times n$ matrix, and let $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℂ}^{n}$ be an eigenvector corresponding to an eigenvalue $\text{λ}$ in $\text{ℂ}$. Show that for each nonzero complex scalar $\mu$, the vector $\mu\textbf{x}$ is an eigenvector of $A$.

exercise_group.instructions: In Exercises 23–26, $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix with real entries, and $\textbf{x}$ is a vector in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) The matrix $A$ can have one real and one complex eigenvalue.
(T/F) The points $A\textbf{x},A^{2}\,\textbf{x},A^{3}\,\textbf{x},\ldots$ always lie on the same circle.
(T/F) The matrix $A$ always has two eigenvalues, but sometimes they have algebraic multiplicity $2$ or are complex numbers.
(T/F) If the matrix $A$ has two complex eigenvalues, then it also has two linearly independent real eigenvectors.
